strengths: Introduces a clever, verifiably novel task (3x3 jigsaw puzzles) that even strong closed-source models like GPT-4o fail on at chance level, providing a clean testbed isolating 'new knowledge acquisition' from 'knowledge already in pretraining corpora', which is a genuine methodological contribution for studying forgetting.

The central empirical finding—that SFT on RFT-generated rollouts (Rea-GRPO-Rollout) can match RFT's task performance while incurring far less forgetting than either non-reasoning SFT or SFT on GPT-4o-generated reasoning traces—is a valuable and somewhat surprising result that reframes the SFT-vs-RFT forgetting debate as a data-distribution issue rather than a purely algorithmic one.

The learning-dynamics framework (via eNTK) that decomposes influence into magnitude and direction, together with the symmetry theorem (Thm 5.2), provides a principled and interpretable causal story for why data lying in low-perplexity regions of the base model interferes less with prior knowledge.

The experimental protocol is reasonably comprehensive: two model scales (3B/7B), multiple data variants (Non-Rea, Rea-4o, Rea-GRPO), and evaluation across five diverse capability axes (grounding, OCR/document, general VQA, hallucination, college-level reasoning), plus supporting analyses (PPL curves, LBK curves, Pareto fronts, qualitative examples) that converge on a consistent story.

Practically relevant insight for continual learning/post-training practice: it suggests concrete, actionable guidance (favor RL-rollout-style data or low-perplexity/reasoning-augmented SFT data) rather than only diagnosing a problem.
weaknesses: The study is confined to a single synthetic task (3x3 jigsaw) and a single model family (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B); the authors themselves note this in limitations, but this substantially limits confidence that 'distribution of training data, rather than algorithmic differences, plays a central role in forgetting' generalizes to other novel tasks, other architectures, or larger scales.

The central causal claim (algorithm vs. data) is somewhat overstated: the fact that low-perplexity, well-aligned rollouts arise specifically because RFT explores the model's own output space means algorithm and data distribution are entangled rather than cleanly separable; the paper would benefit from more explicit discussion of this interdependence rather than framing it as data being the sole factor.

The comparison between Rea-4o-Rollout and Rea-GRPO-Rollout is not fully controlled — these differ not only in perplexity/alignment to the base model but potentially in reasoning quality, style, length, and correctness distribution (rollouts are filtered by correctness at ~65% retention while GPT-4o data presumably is not filtered the same way), leaving open whether perplexity alone, versus other confounds, drives the forgetting difference.

No comparison against standard continual-learning/anti-forgetting baselines (e.g., regularization-based EWC, replay of pretraining-like data, LoRA/parameter-isolation) is provided, which would help contextualize how much RFT's advantage matters relative to existing mitigation techniques.

The theoretical framework relies on the strong assumption that the eNTK matrix remains roughly stable over the fine-tuning trajectory; while this is inherited from prior work (Ren & Sutherland, 2024) on LLM fine-tuning, its validity in a multimodal RFT/GRPO setting with many training steps (up to ~27k) is asserted rather than rigorously verified, and this assumption underlies most of the causal narrative in Sec 5.4-5.5.

Some quantitative results are somewhat noisy or inconsistent with the paper's clean narrative (e.g., Fig 2 shows Rea-4o-Rollout sometimes has smaller LBK than Rea-GRPO-Rollout for the 3B model, yet still forgets more — acknowledged by the authors as due to perplexity, but this weakens the claim that magnitude and direction cleanly separate the two effects), and no statistical significance testing is reported for the main benchmark tables.

RFT training required an extremely long training budget (~27,360 steps, tens of thousands more than SFT) to reach comparable task accuracy, raising practical concerns about the real-world applicability of the 'RFT preserves knowledge better' conclusion when computational parity is considered, and this cost-performance tradeoff is not thoroughly analyzed.
